questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the forearm with a central black eschar and surrounding gelatinous edema. Gram-positive rods are seen on smear. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis presents with a painless ulcer with central black eschar (malignant pustule) and surrounding non-pitting gelatinous edema. Gram-positive spore-forming bacilli are seen on smear.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent man presents with multiple follicular pustules on the trunk that began after a hot-tub session. Culture grows a gram-negative rod. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Hot-tub folliculitis is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It occurs after exposure to inadequately chlorinated water (hot tubs, swimming pools) and presents with follicular pustules predominantly on the trunk.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a honey-colored crusted lesion around the nostrils and mouth. Direct immunofluorescence is not routinely done. Which is the most appropriate first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes is best treated with topical mupirocin, which has excellent gram-positive coverage and low resistance rates. It is the preferred first-line topical agent.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden redness, pain, and swelling of existing skin lesions along with fever. Nerve tenderness is present but there are no new skin lesions. Which reaction is occurring?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. It causes inflammation of existing lesions, neuritis, and can lead to sudden nerve function impairment. No new lesions appear.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy on MDT develops painful erythematous nodules on the arms and legs with fever, arthritis, and iridocyclitis. Which is the treatment of choice for this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) is treated with thalidomide (100–400 mg/day) as first-line due to its anti-TNF-alpha activity. However, in women of childbearing age, thalidomide is contraindicated and prednisolone/clofazimine are used instead.

questions.q: A 19-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Dark-field microscopy is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based chancre at the site of inoculation with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy demonstrating Treponema pallidum spirochetes confirms the diagnosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a painful genital ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain shows 'school of fish' pattern. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and presents with painful, soft, ragged ulcers. Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Tender suppurative inguinal bubo may be present.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple small, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication on the face and trunk. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (caused by a poxvirus) in immunocompromised patients is treated with cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), which is the most commonly used and effective physical modality. Topical imiquimod is an alternative for immunocompetent patients.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with painful vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome for 3 days. Which antiviral drug and dose should be given?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is best treated with valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days. It offers better bioavailability and simpler dosing than acyclovir. Famciclovir 500 mg TDS is another option. Treatment should start within 72 hours of rash onset.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops painful vesicles and crusted plaques in a dermatomal distribution. Two months after the acute episode resolves, she still has persistent burning pain at the site. What is this condition?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is defined as pain persisting for more than 90 days after the herpes zoster rash onset. It is the most common complication of herpes zoster, especially in elderly patients. Treatment includes gabapentin, pregabalin, and tricyclic antidepressants.

questions.q: An 8-year-old child presents with tinea capitis with multiple boggy, fluctuant plaques studded with broken hair stubs, and regional lymphadenopathy. What is this presentation called and what is the treatment?
questions.exp: Kerion is a severe inflammatory form of tinea capitis, typically caused by zoophilic dermatophytes (Trichophyton verrucosum, T. mentagrophytes). It presents as a boggy, suppurative plaque. Treatment requires oral griseofulvin (not topical antifungals) as the fungus is deep in the hair follicle.

questions.q: A 35-year-old immunocompromised patient develops widespread skin lesions with central necrosis. Skin biopsy shows broad, non-septate hyphae branching at right angles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mucormycosis is caused by Mucorales fungi (Rhizopus, Mucor) and shows broad, ribbon-like, non-septate (or pauci-septate) hyphae branching at right angles (90°). Aspergillus shows narrow, septate hyphae branching at 45°. It is seen in diabetics and immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term corticosteroids presents with oral white plaques that can be scraped off leaving a bleeding surface. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast. Which drug is first-line?
questions.exp: Oral candidiasis (thrush) is caused by Candida albicans. First-line treatment is topical nystatin oral suspension (rinse and swallow) or clotrimazole troches for localized disease. Systemic fluconazole is reserved for refractory cases or severe/esophageal involvement.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and inflamed skin, predominantly in flexural areas. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone on DIF. It presents with tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin in elderly patients. Nikolsky sign is negative (unlike pemphigus vulgaris where it is positive).

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with flaccid bullae, erosions, and crusting predominantly on the scalp, face, and upper trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. The antigen target is in which layer of the skin?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein 3 (and sometimes desmoglein 1) within the epidermis. Acantholysis leads to suprabasal split. DIF shows intercellular IgG in a 'fish-net' pattern. Nikolsky sign is positive.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with intensely pruritic papulovesicles symmetrically distributed on elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae. What is the associated systemic condition?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae. Treatment includes dapsone and a gluten-free diet. The skin lesions respond dramatically to dapsone.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with SLE develops a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash on the malar area sparing the nasolabial folds. Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though it has lower sensitivity (~25-30%). Anti-dsDNA has high specificity and correlates with disease activity. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjögren's syndrome.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, and dysphagia. ANA shows anti-centromere antibody pattern. What pattern of systemic sclerosis does this suggest?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies are characteristic of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), previously known as CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with heliotrope discoloration of eyelids, Gottron's papules over MCP joints, and proximal muscle weakness. Which malignancy is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults (especially women over 40) is most commonly associated with ovarian cancer, followed by lung, breast, and gastrointestinal cancers. Gottron's papules and heliotrope rash are pathognomonic. Anti-Mi-2 antibody is associated with classic DM.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectatic vessels and a raised, rolled border on the nose present for 18 months. He has significant sun exposure history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer and presents as a pearly papule/nodule with rolled telangiectatic border on sun-exposed areas (especially nose). It rarely metastasizes but can cause local destruction. Mohs surgery is the treatment of choice for high-risk locations.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing keratotic nodule on the lip that appeared over 6 weeks. The lesion has a central keratin-filled crater. What is the natural history of this lesion if untreated?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing epithelial tumor that characteristically shows spontaneous involution over 3-6 months leaving a scar. However, because it is histologically similar to SCC, excision is generally recommended. Some consider it a well-differentiated SCC variant.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has a suspicious pigmented lesion on the upper back. Dermoscopy shows an asymmetric irregular pigment network and blue-white veil. Excision biopsy shows Breslow thickness of 1.8 mm. What is the recommended surgical margin?
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.01-2.0 mm, the recommended surgical excision margin is 2 cm. For ≤1 mm: 1 cm margin; for 2.01-4 mm: 2 cm; for >4 mm: 2-3 cm. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered for lesions >1 mm thickness.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes patch testing. Reading is done at 48 hours and 96 hours. The reaction at 48 hours shows vesicles, papules, and erythema. What grade of reaction is this on the International Contact Dermatitis Research Group (ICDRG) scale?
questions.exp: ICDRG patch test grading: Negative (-): no reaction; Doubtful (+?): faint erythema only; Weak positive (1+): non-vesicular erythema, infiltrate, papules; Strong positive (2+): erythema, infiltrate, papules, vesicles; Extreme positive (3+): intense erythema, coalescing vesicles, bullae.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman wants laser treatment for her café-au-lait macules. Which laser type is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Q-switched lasers (Nd:YAG 532 nm, ruby 694 nm, alexandrite 755 nm) are used for pigmented lesions including café-au-lait macules. The Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm targets melanin in epidermal lesions. Pulsed dye laser targets oxyhemoglobin (vascular lesions).

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a Tzanck smear from the floor of a vesicle in a patient with suspected herpes simplex. What is the characteristic finding?
opts: Neutrophilic infiltrate with no specific cells
Multinucleated giant cells with steel-gray nuclei
questions.exp: Tzanck smear in herpes simplex (and herpes zoster) shows multinucleated giant cells (syncytia) with steel-gray 'ground glass' nuclei and nuclear molding. This distinguishes herpetic from non-herpetic vesicles but cannot differentiate HSV from VZV.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with moderate plaque psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Which baseline investigation is most important before starting treatment?
opts: Complete blood count, LFT, RFT, and chest X-ray
questions.exp: Before starting methotrexate, baseline CBC (for bone marrow suppression), LFTs, RFTs (methotrexate is renally excreted; renal impairment increases toxicity), and chest X-ray (for pulmonary status) are essential. Liver biopsy is no longer routinely required at baseline; it may be indicated after cumulative dose of 3.5-4 g.

questions.q: A patient on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops pallor, jaundice, and methemoglobinemia. What is the most appropriate antidote for methemoglobinemia?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Methemoglobinemia is treated with IV methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg), which acts as a cofactor for NADPH-methemoglobin reductase to reduce methemoglobin to hemoglobin. It is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman is prescribed isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne. After 1 month she presents with elevated triglycerides (450 mg/dL). What is the appropriate action?
opts: Continue isotretinoin and add dietary modifications only
Reduce isotretinoin dose and add fenofibrate
questions.exp: Isotretinoin can elevate triglycerides. If triglycerides exceed 400-500 mg/dL, the dose should be reduced. A fibrate (fenofibrate) is added for persistent hypertriglyceridemia. Isotretinoin is stopped only if triglycerides exceed 800 mg/dL or pancreatitis develops. Statins are avoided due to myopathy risk.

questions.q: The Langerhans cell is the principal antigen-presenting cell in the epidermis. Which electron microscopy finding is characteristic of Langerhans cells?
questions.exp: Langerhans cells contain Birbeck granules, which are tennis racket-shaped structures seen on electron microscopy. They express CD1a, CD207 (langerin), and S100. Langerin (CD207) is responsible for Birbeck granule formation and is a marker used in immunohistochemistry.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with palpable purpura on the lower limbs, arthralgias, and haematuria is found to have cryoglobulinemia. Which hepatitis virus is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Mixed cryoglobulinemia (Type II and III) is strongly associated with Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in approximately 80-90% of cases. HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis presents with the classic triad of palpable purpura, arthralgias, and weakness. Treatment targets HCV with antiviral therapy.
